correctness.rationale: Complementation reduces to s≤n/2 without changing either dimension. Every root query has exactly s positive centers, so complete depth d requires 2^(d−1)≤s. On m≤s consecutive centers, query u+t−1 to split the first t from the rest: the two involved integer blocks fit in an interval of at most s+m≤n points, so cyclic reduction creates no extra positive centers. After the initial split both branches contain a block of 2^floor(log₂ s) centers, each bisected recursively; this also handles s=1 with depth-zero children. Adjacent points yield all four traces if s≥2, but a triple inside an s-arc cannot realize the two outer positives without its middle point, since the opposite circular path needs at least n−s+1 edges. For s=1 the singleton class shatters a point but not a pair. Taking s=floor(n/2) gives the claimed maximum with the stated attainment threshold. Independently validated every path of the supplied data-only n=128,k=64 witness: 128 leaves of depth seven, all distinct centers, each satisfying its entire path.
residual_risks: The single independently replayed certificate establishes only the finite witness, not the general formula. The other reported finite recurrence runs were not independently repeated.

value.rationale: The exact width-dependent online dimension is a useful calibration for a natural translate class: despite VC dimension at most two, it ranges from one to the whole-class information bound. The theorem says exactly when that bound is attained and provides a constructive witness; its contribution is not just computing the largest certificate or exhibiting some VC/Littlestone separation already available from other classes.
residual_risks: The result is for uniform lengths with all translates; no general claim about disconnected supports or online randomized performance follows.
